summaries.example: Imagine a game where you receive three puzzle pieces and must use them to finish a picture. In an ordinary game, an extra piece might not hurt. In a resource-style logic, the extra piece may matter: it could make the reasoning no longer fit the rules. In another system, the order of the pieces could matter, or a piece could be used only once. These different choices change which conclusions count as following from the starting pieces.
summaries.summary: Substructural logics are families of logical systems that do not all accept the usual rules for handling premises. A structural rule is a general rule about premises or conclusions: it may allow an extra premise, let premises change order, group them in different ways, or permit a premise to be reused. Substructural logics study what happens when one or more of these rules is removed or restricted. Relevant logics emphasize that premises should help support the conclusion. Linear logic treats premises as limited resources that cannot be used again and again. The Lambek calculus applies similar ideas to language, where the order and combination of words matter. Other systems change rules connecting one sequent to another, such as Cut or Identity. Researchers study these logics by examining formal proofs and by building models that show when arguments succeed or fail. The main lesson is that changing the background rules for combining premises can change the behavior of familiar logical connectives, including “if,” “and,” and “or.”
key_ideas: Substructural logics are logical systems that leave out, limit, or change some usual structural rules.
The rules can say whether premises may be added, switched, grouped differently, or reused.
Some systems care about relevance, so an unrelated premise cannot simply be added.
Linear logic treats premises more like resources: they must be used and cannot be reused freely.
The Lambek calculus studies ordered combinations of language pieces, so changing their order can change the result.
Proofs and models are two ways to study why a conclusion follows.
summaries.why_it_matters: Substructural logics show that reasoning is shaped not only by the meanings of words such as “if” and “not,” but also by how we manage the information used in an argument. This helps philosophers and mathematicians describe relevance, limited resources, word order, computer processes, and some difficult logical puzzles. It also teaches an important lesson: small changes in the rules for combining information can create very different kinds of reasoning.

important_terms.definition: A system for deciding which conclusions follow from which starting statements.
A rule about how statements may be arranged, added, moved, or reused, regardless of their special topic.
A substructural rule that allows an extra premise to be added even when it is not needed.
A rule that allows a premise to be used more than once, or treats repeated uses as one use.
A statement or group of statements used to support a conclusion.
The sign or relation meaning that a conclusion follows from premises; it is often written as a turnstile.

questions_to_think_about: Should adding an unrelated fact ever change a correct argument?
If two premises are written in a different order, should they always mean the same thing?
When might it be important to use a clue only once?
Is a rule about arranging premises different from a rule about what words such as “not” or “if” mean?

summaries.example: Suppose a computer process has two available resources, A and B. In ordinary classical reasoning, if A is enough to establish C, then adding B normally leaves C established. A resource-sensitive logic may reject that step because B has not been used appropriately. A linear system may also reject moving from A,A ⊢ C to A ⊢ C: using A twice is not the same as using it once. A language-oriented system may reject rearranging A,B as B,A, because order represents composition. The same conditional can therefore behave differently in different logical environments.
summaries.summary: Substructural logics investigate logical systems by focusing on structural rules: rules that govern the general organization of premises and conclusions. Classical logic permits weakening, contraction, exchange of order, and ordinary grouping of premises, along with rules such as Cut and Identity. A substructural logic may reject or restrict any of these. Without weakening, an inference supported by X need not remain supported after adding Y; this fits the idea that a conclusion should depend on relevant premises. Without contraction, X,X ⊢ A need not imply X ⊢ A, which models limited resources and motivates linear logic. Without commutativity or associativity, the order or grouping of premises affects what follows, as in the Lambek calculus for syntax. The choice of structural rules also affects the behavior of conditionals and other connectives. Proof-theoretic presentations use formal rules to build derivations, while model-theoretic presentations use points, relations, or valuations to represent validity. Some systems are decidable because proof search can be bounded, although not every substructural logic has that property. The entry also discusses quantifiers, whose proof rules are comparatively clear but whose semantic treatment can be difficult. Finally, systems such as ST and TS remove Cut or Identity, showing that a logic’s distinctive character may appear not only in its valid sequents but also in relationships between sequents.
key_ideas: Structural rules describe the background behavior of consequence, while operational rules describe particular connectives, quantifiers, or negation.
Rejecting weakening supports relevance: adding material can invalidate an inference because the added material may not contribute to the conclusion.
Rejecting contraction supports resource sensitivity, as in linear logic, where a premise cannot be freely reused.
Rejecting commutativity or associativity makes order or grouping significant; this is important in the Lambek calculus and related theories of language.
Proof theory studies formal derivations, while model theory studies structures in which formulas are evaluated; both can explain structural behavior.
Cut-free and identity-free systems show that even rules connecting premises and conclusions can be altered, producing non-transitive or unusually sparse consequence relations.
summaries.why_it_matters: Substructural logic provides a precise way to study assumptions that ordinary logic often leaves in the background. It connects relevance, resource use, linguistic composition, proof search, semantics, and the treatment of paradoxes. It also clarifies that classical logic can be understood as a system with a particularly generous collection of structural rules. Comparing systems helps us see which conclusions depend on the meanings of logical vocabulary and which depend on the general architecture of consequence.

important_terms.definition: A non-classical logic characterized by rejecting or restricting one or more structural rules of classical consequence.
A general rule governing the context of consequence rather than the special form of a connective or quantifier.
The rule allowing premises to be added without affecting an existing derivation: from X ⊢ A, infer X,Y ⊢ A.
The rule allowing repeated premises to be collapsed: from X,X ⊢ A, infer X ⊢ A.
The rule allowing the order of combined premises to be exchanged.
The rule treating different parenthesizations of premise combination as equivalent.
A rule connecting a derivation of an intermediate formula with a later derivation that uses it; rejecting it makes consequence non-transitive.
The basic sequent B ⊢ B, which gives a proof system a starting connection between a formula as premise and as conclusion.

questions_to_think_about: Is an argument still relevant when an unrelated premise is added to it?
What is lost, and what is gained, when a premise cannot be reused?
How could word order be represented by a non-commutative logic?
Why might a proof system be useful even when its valid sequents resemble those of another system?
Can a logic handle a paradox by refusing a general rule for combining two valid steps?

summaries.example: Think about planning a group project. In one reasoning system, if your plan works with the materials already listed, adding another material cannot make the conclusion fail. That is similar to weakening. In a different system, the new material might have to be genuinely relevant. If the plan needs one copy of a tool, using two copies may not be equivalent to using one; this resembles the rejection of contraction. And if the order of steps matters, then “step A followed by step B” is not the same as “step B followed by step A.” Substructural logics explore these differences formally.
summaries.summary: Substructural logics are non-classical systems defined by their treatment of structural rules. These rules govern the general behavior of consequence: whether premises may be added, rearranged, regrouped, or duplicated, and how formulas on opposite sides of a sequent are connected. Weakening permits an extra premise to be introduced. Contraction permits repeated use to be reduced to a single use. Commutativity permits reordering, while associativity permits changes in grouping. Cut chains two stages of reasoning, and Identity supplies the basic link from a formula to itself. Removing one of these rules changes what can be inferred. Relevant logics restrict premise combination to preserve dependence on useful information. Linear logic interprets premises as resources, so they cannot be copied without limit. The Lambek calculus treats premise combination like the composition of linguistic units, making order important. The field also includes proof systems and semantic models, and it studies how quantifiers behave when the usual structural assumptions are unavailable. Work on logics without Cut or Identity shows that a system may resemble classical logic at the level of individual sequents while differing in how sequents relate to one another.
key_ideas: Classical logic uses several broad rules for adding, rearranging, grouping, and repeating premises.
Relevant logics may reject weakening because an unrelated premise should not become part of a support relation merely by being added.
Linear logic treats assumptions as resources that must be used and cannot be copied indefinitely.
The Lambek calculus models language and syntax, where both the number and order of combined units can matter.
Different choices about structural rules can produce different conditionals, including direction-sensitive ones.
Proof theory examines how conclusions can be derived; model theory examines situations or structures that make arguments valid or invalid.
summaries.why_it_matters: This subject reveals that logic is not only a collection of rules for words like “and,” “or,” and “if.” It also depends on a background theory of how reasons are combined. That insight is useful for analyzing relevance, language, limited resources, proof-search algorithms, and certain paradoxes. It gives students a way to compare logical systems without assuming that classical logic’s structural habits are unavoidable.

important_terms.definition: A family of non-classical logics that changes some general rules for combining premises or conclusions.
A rule that applies to the surrounding collection of premises, not to a particular connective such as “and” or “if.”
Allowing an extra premise to be added while keeping the same conclusion.
Allowing a premise that appears twice to be treated as though it appeared once.
Allowing the order of premises to be switched without changing what follows.
Allowing different ways of grouping premises to count as the same arrangement.
A general chaining rule: if A leads to B and B leads to C, then A leads to C.
The basic principle that a statement follows from itself, written B ⊢ B.

questions_to_think_about: Would adding information ever make an argument less acceptable? Explain why a relevance-based logic might say yes.
Is copying a resource the same as using it twice?
Why might a grammar need a logic in which A,B differs from B,A?
What could happen if the usual chaining rule, Cut, were not always allowed?
Should two logics count as the same if they prove the same individual sequents but connect those sequents differently?
